newsitem.title: CHINA: HK analysts welcome China bourse centralisation.
newsitem.headline: HK analysts welcome China bourse centralisation.

text.p: China's move to put its stock exchanges under the direct control of the central government was welcomed in Hong Kong on Friday, but had no impact on trading in the territory, brokers and analysts said.

"It's a healthy process, giving better control and regulation of the China market. But the influence on the Hong Kong stock market is probably minimal as Hong Kong has its own regulations," said Vickers Ballas sales director Antony Mak.
China's State Council has ordered the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) to take direct control over the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges, state media said on Friday.
The move follows a series of measures by Beijing to crack down on excessive speculation in local markets.
Analysts said it would improve market supervision.
"China is a relatively developing country so you don't expect the people to understand fully the significance of complying with regulations," said one Hong Kong analyst.

While any measures to control liquidity might impact share prices in the territory, where China-related red chips have benefited from an inflow of mainland money, analysts said they did not see China's latest step as a sign that Beijing would interfere directly with the Hong Kong stock market.
"I don't think they will implement restrictions or intervention in the day-to-day Hong Kong Stock Exchange," said Keith Wu, head of research at Peregrine Securities.

Mainland moves to control injections of mainland assets into red chip companies only briefly dampened sentiment in the red chip sector earlier this year and Hong Kong analysts also viewed that move as ultimately a positive one.
"What they will do is make sure that any China-related asset injections or listing of PRC (People's Republic of China) enterprises would be very much monitored by the CSRC," said Wu.
Analysts said China would generate more confidence in its market by ensuring regulations were complied with, and that would be more easily achieved with central supervision.
"I think they will put the stock exchanges in order. You need someone strong enough to enforce regulations," said Frederick Tsang, head of research at BNP PrimeEast Securities.
"The stock exchange is very crucial for China to raise foreign funds," he added.
Andrew Kuet, an analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said it was a step forward in centralising management of the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges.
"The advantage is this will turn the markets into truly nationalised markets from regional bourses." he said.
Hong Kong's blue chip Hang Seng Index ended the morning session down 151.67 points, or 0.92 percent, at 16,346.04, hit by profit-taking ahead of a long weekend in the territory.
B shares soared on the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges.
The Shanghai B share index was up 7.469, or 9.28 percent, at 87.965 and the Shenzhen B share index gained 11.12 points, or 7.35 percent, to 162.34.
